chunks: Push-pull vs open-drain trade-offs. The question: What are the two most common types of GPIO implementations? What are their tradeoffs?
A GPIO output can be push-pull or open-drain. A push-pull pin actively drives both high and low, so its edges are fast and it needs no extra parts.
An open-drain pin can only pull low or let go. A resistor, called a pull-up, brings it high when released. Push-pull is faster.
Open-drain lets several devices safely share one wire.
Picture a bathtub. A push-pull pin is a tub with a big filling tap and a big drain. It fills and empties quickly.
But if two people share the tub, one with the tap open and one with the drain open, water just pours straight through, wasted.
An open-drain pin is a tub with only drain plugs and a trickle tap. Anyone can pull a plug without a fight. The price is slow refilling.
Left: push-pull, two transistors, the output follows the input actively.
Right: open-drain, one transistor and an external pull-up: the NMOS pulls the line down when its gate is high, and the resistor pulls it up when the NMOS is off.
(The "in" drive polarity is inverted in the right figure; a real pin hides this in its logic.)
Push-pull: an output with two switches, one driving high and one driving low. Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch. It pulls low or lets go.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that brings an open-drain line high when nobody pulls it low. Wired-AND: a shared open-drain line that is low if any device pulls it low.
Rise time: how long the wire takes to climb from low to high. Capacitance: the charge a wire stores. It must be filled before the voltage can rise, like a bucket.
Take a 3. 3 volts line with 100 picofarads of capacitance. A push-pull pin with a 25 ohms switch charges it in a few nanoseconds ( 25 ohms times 100 picofarads equals 2.
5 nanoseconds). An open-drain pin with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up takes about 400 nanoseconds to climb from 30% to 70%. Whenever it holds the line low, that pull-up draws 3.
3 over 4700 equals 0. 70 milliamps. A 10 kilohms pull-up draws less, 0. 33 milliamps, but the rise stretches to about 850 nanoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"The two types are push-pull and open-drain. Push-pull has a PMOS and NMOS and drives both high and low: fast edges, no static current, but two drivers on one line fight.
Open-drain only pulls low and needs an external pull-up for high: the rise is an RC curve, about 400 nanoseconds for 4.
7 kilohms and 100 picofarads, and it burns current when low.
But devices can share the line safely as a wired-AND, and the pull-up can be at a different voltage for level translation.
So push-pull for point-to-point speed, open-drain for shared buses like I2C and interrupt lines."
